extracted.intended_audience: OSHA stakeholders: employers, occupational safety and health professionals, researchers, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and assessing evidence on heat-related health effects, case definitions, risk factors, injury classification, and intervention effectiveness to inform a proposed OSHA heat standard. Includes diagnostic criteria, mechanisms, limitations of studies, and policy-relevant conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute kidney injury (AKI) case definition and measurement limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of serum creatinine measures taken over relatively short spans of time may be too short to see true reductions in GFR; short-term fluctuations in serum creatinine may be due to reductions in renal blood flow (e.g., dehydration) and not necessarily indicative of clinically significant structural injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret cross-shift or short-term creatinine changes with caution. Consider that transient/prerenal changes can mimic AKI on short timescales; longer-term measures or repeated tests may be needed to distinguish reversible/dehydration-related changes from structural kidney injury. See discussion referenced for chronic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum of AKI severity and recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: AKI ranges in severity; some individuals are asymptomatic and detectable only by serum or urine tests; biomarkers of AKI can return to baseline quickly in some cases, while intrarenal causes may require longer recovery and possibly medication or dialysis. AKI from heat stroke can be irreversible and fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating AKI, account for variation in symptom visibility and recovery time. Distinguish transient (rapidly reversible) AKI from sustained/intrarenal AKI that may require medical interventions and may predispose to chronic kidney disease (CKD). Recurrent AKI should be regarded as a risk factor for CKD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) diagnostic criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: CKD is typically diagnosed when the estimated GFR is below a rate of 60 mL/min/1.73m2 for at least 3 months, although there are other indicators, like a high albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated measurements over months to years to establish CKD (not single short-term tests). Recognize stages of CKD, with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) defined as kidney failure requiring dialysis or transplant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence linking occupational heat exposure to CKD
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational studies (e.g., sugarcane worker cohorts) find associations between cross-shift increases in serum creatinine or severe short-term fluctuations and subsequent declines in estimated GFR over weeks to a year; intervention studies in Central America show that water-rest-shade controls are associated with reduced declines in kidney function and reduced rates of kidney injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both observational longitudinal data and intervention studies when assessing causality. Note population differences (Central America vs. U.S.), potential co-exposures (agrichemicals, infectious agents), and study limitations (follow-up length, surveillance gaps). Positive intervention effects strengthen causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and biases in occupational kidney studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations include healthy worker effect, limited long-term follow-up (months vs. years), potential reverse causality (undiagnosed CKD causing AKI), geographic/population differences, and limited surveillance of susceptible worker groups (e.g., migrant workers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate studies for possible selection bias, confounding exposures, inadequate follow-up duration, and surveillance gaps. Use caution when extrapolating findings across different worker populations; account for alternative nephrotoxic exposures and data quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and prognosis for CKD and AKI
rubrics_metrics.description: CKD is progressive and can worsen over time with scarring; late-stage CKD (ESRD) requires dialysis or transplant and is permanent. AKI recovery varies—some return to baseline quickly while others may need prolonged treatment or dialysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing health burden from occupational heat, include long-term outcomes (ESRD, dialysis, transplant) and acknowledge permanent disability risk. Consider how even early-stage CKD can increase susceptibility to heat-related illness at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and classification of heat-related injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: A heat-related injury means an injury, such as a fall or cut, that is linked to heat exposure (may result from a heat-related illness). Identification/classification varies case-by-case because mechanisms differ (impaired reaction time, vision, dexterity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no specific ICD or OIICS codes just for heat-related injuries; to attribute an injury to heat, combine a heat-related OIICS/ICD code with an injury OIICS/ICD code. Expect case-by-case assessment and use both illness and injury codes where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual-level risk factors for heat-related illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous factors can affect response to heat stress, including genotype and gene expression, body mass, biological sex, age (including healthy aging effects), pregnancy, chronic conditions (cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes), obesity, prior heat illness, and recent or concurrent acute illness or infection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize heterogeneity in susceptibility across workers. Although these factors affect risk, OSHA states the proposed standard's application does not depend on employer knowledge of individual susceptibilities. When analyzing risk, consider prevalence of these factors and potential effect modification, but be aware evidence is often not robust enough to quantify their relative contributions or combined effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medications and clinical conditions that modify thermoregulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many medications can decrease thermoregulatory capability (e.g., antipsychotics, dopaminergics, opioids, amphetamines; anticholinergics, antihypertensives, antiplatelets, some antidepressants and antihistamines, aspirin) and can affect perception of heat, electrolyte balance, kidney function, hydration, or cardiac output (e.g., diuretics, ACE inhibitors, some anti-diabetics, beta-blockers, NSAIDs, tricyclics, laxatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering worker risk, account for common prescription medication use in working-age adults and specific classes known to impair heat response. Refer to NIOSH, Department of the Army, and CDC guidance (tables cited) for detailed class-specific mechanisms. Employers are not expected to base compliance on individual medication lists, but clinicians and occupational health professionals should consider these interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illicit and legal substances affecting heat risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Amphetamines (prescription or illicit), methamphetamines, cocaine, alcohol, and heavy caffeine use (e.g., energy drinks) can impair thermoregulation, increase heat generation, or promote dehydration; these substances have been implicated in heat-related fatalities and increased risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider substance use as an important risk factor in fatality analyses and in assessing worker risk profiles. Data limitations (small samples, incomplete toxicology, uncertainty about prescription vs non-prescription use) constrain precise quantification; nonetheless, evidence supports that these substances can substantially increase heat-related risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence quality considerations for reproductive and developmental effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There is mixed but suggestive evidence that heat exposure affects reproductive and developmental outcomes (infertility, teratogenicity, pre-term birth, low birth weight), with mechanisms proposed from animal studies and some human epidemiology; many occupational studies are cross-sectional or rely on self-report or occupation categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reproductive/developmental findings as suggestive; prioritize studies with direct exposure quantification and longitudinal designs. Recognize limitations from recall bias, exposure misclassification, and inability of cross-sectional studies to establish causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term health effects following prior heat illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospective and cohort studies suggest prior exertional heat illness or heat stroke may be associated with higher long-term incidence of cardiovascular events and chronic kidney disease, but the body of research is limited and subject to confounding and retrospective data limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating long-term sequelae of heat illness, account for study design limitations (retrospective, possible unmeasured confounders) and treat results as indicative but not definitive; further prospective research is needed to establish causality and magnitude of long-term risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy stance on individual susceptibilities versus population protection
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA reiterates that exposure to workplace heat contributes to heat stress for all workers regardless of individual risk factors and that the proposed standard's application is not dependent on an employer's knowledge or analysis of individual workers' risk factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory decisions and standards should focus on protecting the workforce as a whole rather than tailoring compliance requirements to individual susceptibility. Use knowledge of risk-factor prevalence to inform policy rationale and burden estimates, but not as a basis to deny protections to specific subgroups.
